nodes.text: The host runs a single process, and at most one turn writes a given conversation at a time; an in-process per-conversation lock is enough.
Histories stay bounded (max_history_turns defaults to 20), so rewriting the whole conversation record once per completed turn is cheap.
The default tools are free of external side effects; a host that registers effectful tools makes them idempotent, so replaying a failed turn from the last saved turn is acceptable.
Provider-reported token usage is accurate enough for a soft cap; exact billing is reconciled by the host against the provider.

The platform message models (including ImageDocument and AudioDocument bytes) round-trip through JSON only if the codec sets ser_json_bytes and val_json_bytes to base64 (or the fields use Base64Bytes); pydantic defaults both to utf8. The locked pydantic is 2.13.4, which has val_json_bytes (added in 2.9).

Each of the six LLM adapters can map vendor errors into request-scoped permanent (bad request, context length, content policy), provider-scoped permanent (auth, permission, model not found) and transient errors.

Pydantic-AI UsageLimits offers cost_limit (USD Decimal), request_limit, tool_calls_limit, input_tokens_limit, output_tokens_limit, total_tokens_limit and per_request_input_tokens_limit; all except request_limit default to None.

nodes.text: Pydantic-AI request_limit defaults to 50, and a default UsageLimits() is created when none is passed, so a request cap is ON by default (not zero-config opt-in). It counts model responses committed to history, not retries or fallback attempts. Setting a limit to None disables it.

Pydantic-AI enforces limits at two points: check_before_request (request count, and projected input/total tokens/cost) before each model call, and check_tokens after each response. Both raise the typed UsageLimitExceeded; tool-call limits use check_before_tool_call. H4 is confirmed on enforcement points.

Pydantic-AI pre-request token enforcement is opt-in: count_tokens_before_request=False by default, because it costs an extra token-counting call and is supported only for Anthropic, Google, Bedrock Converse and OpenAI Responses. Otherwise input/output/total token limits trip only after the response that crossed them (overshoot by one response).

nodes.text: When a Pydantic-AI limit trips, the run raises UsageLimitExceeded instead of returning a result, but the crossing response is kept in the run's captured messages with state='interrupted', so partial history is recoverable via capture_run_messages and can be resumed.

Pydantic-AI UsageLimits is scoped to a single run(); a longer period needs the earlier usage carried in via the usage= parameter (a RunUsage accumulated across runs) or a harness SpendLimits capability. H4's per-conversation part is confirmed in mechanism, though the exact check-against-shared-usage semantics were read only from docs prose.

It gates before each request, records spend after each response, raises SpendLimitExceeded (a UsageLimitExceeded subclass), and can overshoot: the crossing request completes and concurrent runs can both pass the check.

nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK has no token, cost or tool-call cap: usage is tracked per run for monitoring only, each Runner.run returns usage for that run alone, and sessions do not carry usage. Its only limit is max_turns (LLM calls in the loop) raising MaxTurnsExceeded; max_turns=None disables it. H5 confirmed for the SDK.

nodes.text: LangGraph caps only graph steps (super-steps) via config recursion_limit, raising GraphRecursionError; default 10,007 since 1.1.4 (10,000 for 1.0.6-1.1.3). It has no built-in token or cost limit, and the docs do not say what state is preserved when it trips. H5 confirmed.

Design inference: a library should offer an opt-in limits object checked before each model call (request/step count, projected tokens/cost) and after each response, raising one typed exception that carries the partial messages, with a caller-owned usage accumulator passed between runs for conversation scope. Pydantic-AI is the closest model; its non-zero request_limit default and after-the-fact token checks are the weak points, and OpenAI/LangGraph offer only turn/step caps.

Metadata/title updates do not change the revision.

nodes.text: LangGraph BaseCheckpointSaver exposes get_tuple, put, put_writes, list, delete_thread (plus async variants); default serde is JsonPlusSerializer; the Checkpoint dict carries an integer format version field v. The unit stored is a graph-state snapshot, not a message log, so it is coupled to graph state schema.

Across the three libraries the host owns the session/thread id and authorization; none enforces isolation itself except optional scope= in Pydantic AI. Only Pydantic AI documents optimistic conflict detection for concurrent turns; OpenAI only locks individual operations.

Design implication: for host embedding, the simplest protocol is item-level async (OpenAI shape: get/add/pop/clear), while Pydantic AI's revisioned record+entries log is the more robust concurrency design; a provider-neutral, version-tagged envelope for stored messages is something none of the three documents fully.

LangGraph's BaseCheckpointSaver protocol is put (checkpoint + metadata + new channel versions), put_writes (intermediate per-task writes), get_tuple (returns CheckpointTuple or None, pending_writes in writes_sort_key order) and list (filter, before, limit), each with an async twin (aput, aput_writes, aget_tuple, alist), plus get_next_version (monotonic, default int +1). Base methods raise NotImplementedError until a saver implements them.

LangGraph durability has three modes: exit (persist only when the graph exits, so a mid-run crash is unrecoverable), async (persist while the next step runs, so the latest checkpoint can be lost on a crash) and sync (persist before the next step starts, highest durability, some cost).
On resume from a super-step, LangGraph keeps pending writes of nodes that completed in that super-step, so completed nodes are not re-run. Resume granularity is the node/super-step, not mid-node.

Recommended: deprecate before delete, rename in stages, stamp a version flag at thread start.

nodes.text: Pydantic-AI replaced graph persistence with a Harness capability StepPersistence: an async StepStore Protocol (about ten methods) with InMemory, File, Sqlite, Mongo and Postgres backends. Snapshots of message history are written after each tool-call step whose calls have all returned and on failure; continue_run returns the latest complete snapshot's messages, fork_run branches, a missing snapshot raises LookupError, and an in-flight step is not retried automatically (tool effects stay 'started' in a ledger). Snapshots exclude mid-step state, capability state and workspace files.

StepPersistence stores JSON (files: run.json, events.jsonl, snapshots/{seq}.json; SQLite with messages keyed by SHA-256) with a content-addressed media marker whose format is versioned; compatibility is upgrade-only and an unknown marker version raises ValueError. Old SQLite DBs get new columns on open (additive migration on open).

Pydantic-AI delegates whole-run crash survival to durable execution engines (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate and others): the engine journals model requests and wrapped tool calls, replays completed steps after restart and retries the in-flight one; non-durable tools run in workflow code on each replay and must be deterministic.

nodes.limitations: Absence of a store was inferred from two docs pages; RunState schema versioning not checked. The HITL page itself does not mention Temporal/DBOS; the running-agents page does.
nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK has no checkpoint store protocol in the pages read: RunState is a serializable snapshot (to_json/to_string, from_json/from_string, result.to_state(), resume via Runner.run(agent, state)) used for paused runs (approvals) and cancel(mode="after_turn"); the application owns storage. Docs warn to deserialize only trusted snapshots. Durable engines (Temporal, DBOS, Dapr, Restate) are external integrations.

Common pattern across the three libraries: checkpoint at a completed-step boundary and keep the store interface small and async (LangGraph: put/put_writes/get_tuple/list; Pydantic-AI: about ten-method StepStore; OpenAI: app-owned RunState blob), and delegate whole-run durability to external durable engines. Pydantic-AI deliberately dropped arbitrary graph-state checkpointing because of parallel execution.

For a single-instance host, a core checkpoint protocol should be minimal: save(run_id, step snapshot), latest(run_id), list/history and writes keyed by (run_id, step_id), JSON-only serialization with an explicit schema-version field and no pickle by default, and a reference SQLite/file backend; defer pending-writes (parallel branches) and durability modes unless parallel nodes are supported.

nodes.text: Core should own one transient/permanent classifier (timeout, connection, 429, 5xx, overloaded = transient; 400, 401/403, 404, context-length = permanent). Retry only transient errors in one layer (set SDK max_retries to 0 or own it, not both). The fallback chain should move on transient errors and provider-side permanent errors (auth, model not found) but not on caller errors (400 bad request, context length), by passing an explicit predicate rather than the permissive library defaults.

MCP lifecycle: wrap each server startup in an explicit timeout (init handshake about 5 s), set a separate per-call timeout, own each client in one dedicated task or an AsyncExitStack entered and exited by the same task, clean up in reverse order, and drop failed servers instead of failing the host.

nodes.applicability: LangGraph per-step checkpointing; one user report plus peer replies, no maintainer statement. Does not apply to a store that saves one record per completed turn.
nodes.limitations: Replies came from community members, not LangGraph maintainers. Web-search snippets also mention a 40GB-in-six-weeks postmortem on Towards AI, which could not be fetched (403) and is not cited.
nodes.text: LangGraph PostgresSaver users report the checkpoint_blobs table growing much faster than the checkpoints table, because the whole messages channel is rewritten each step. Retention needs explicit prune/TTL work. A library that persists full state per step needs a retention and compaction story from day one.

nodes.applicability: LangGraph JsonPlusSerializer; single user report with a contributor's explanation, not a maintainer statement.
nodes.text: A library upgrade that hardens the checkpoint serializer can make previously storable objects (exceptions, non-Serializable custom objects) fail to serialize. The LangGraph langgraph-checkpoint 3.0.0 change was a deliberate security fix, so custom objects in stored state are a compatibility liability.

nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI; the changelog shows compat is maintained, not that it breaks. Partly supports the hypothesis that stored histories need versioning or tolerant loading, but no broken-upgrade bug report was found.
nodes.text: Pydantic AI guarantees only that V1-serialized message history deserializes in V2. It still changes stored-part semantics between releases: RetryPromptPart is no longer written, old retry parts are reinterpreted on load, and the first request after an upgrade misses the provider prompt cache. A library-owned message format changes over time, and the maintainers need an explicit load-compat layer.

nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI UsageLimits and SpendLimits; two pages from one vendor's docs, so not independent. This is what the documentation states, not a user-reported failure.
nodes.limitations: Same-vendor sources. The count_tokens_before_request detail comes from a summary of the page; the quoted sentence is the verbatim part.
nodes.text: Pydantic AI token limits are checked after each model response. The request that crosses the line still completes and is billed, unless count_tokens_before_request=True is set for the per-request input limit. Concurrent runs can each pass the check before any records usage. A cap is therefore a soft bound, not a hard ceiling.

nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI SpendLimits (harness); vendor documentation of its own limitation.
nodes.text: A stream stopped part-way is charged only for the usage the provider had reported by then, which can fall short of the provider's bill. Known token totals for incomplete usage are lower bounds. Reconcile against the provider for exact totals.

nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI usage docs.
nodes.text: In Pydantic AI, request_limit bounds agent-loop turns, not provider requests. Fallback attempts and provider retries do not count toward it, but their tokens and cost still count toward token and cost limits. A fallback chain therefore multiplies spend inside token caps, and a request-count cap does not bound it.

nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI FallbackModel; maintainer replies in a GitHub issue. Does not show fallback masking real bugs.
nodes.text: FallbackModel cannot recover from failures above it, such as output parsing or validation failures. A maintainer said it 'cannot automatically retry things that happen upstream from it'. A model-level fallback chain does not cover real-world failure modes that occur after the response is received.

nodes.applicability: OpenAI Agents SDK sessions with streaming, stop_on_first_tool and output guardrails; a narrow path, fixed upstream.
nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK streamed runs had a bug where a tripped output guardrail dropped the function_call/function_call_output pair from the saved session. The next run re-issued the call and the tool ran twice. This is a duplicated side effect caused by session persistence at turn level, fixed in PR 4148.

nodes.applicability: General durable-execution argument from a practitioner blog; no measurement or incident data.
nodes.limitations: Unrecorded-effect and replay parts independently reproduced (OpenAI SDK issues, Pydantic AI docs); the idempotency-key-source part rests on one industry blog.
nodes.text: A crash between a committed external effect and the checkpoint write makes resume repeat the effect, for example a duplicate refund. Checkpoints alone do not make tools safe; the idempotency key must come from durable run state, not the model.

nodes.applicability: SQLiteSession, thread-level safety; does not show two async turns on one session_id being serialized.
nodes.limitations: Content from a PR description summary, not the diff.
nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK SQLiteSession created a new lock on every call for file-based databases, so it had no thread safety for file DBs. Only in-memory DBs used the shared lock. A shipped session store therefore lacked concurrency protection until a later fix.

nodes.applicability: LangChain agents, a forum post; the reply was not from a maintainer.
nodes.text: LangChain agents' built-in limiters cap call count, not tokens, so a few large calls can consume a very large token volume. Users asked for a token budget. A call-count cap is not a spend cap.

Hypothesis 2 holds: post-response token checks let a single call exceed the cap, so opt-in caps need a pre-request estimate (or a hard per-request max_tokens) if they must be hard, and the typed error must say the cap was crossed by the last call. Docs should say the cap is soft.

Hypothesis 3 is supported but needs refinement. Save-after-completed-turn loses effects of an interrupted turn, and tool side effects can be duplicated on replay (crash window; PR 4148 guardrail path). The design should require idempotency keys for effectful tools, persist tool call and result pairs atomically, and document that a failed turn is replayed from the last saved turn.

Hypothesis 1 is only partly supported. Evidence shows format changes (Pydantic AI retry parts, LangGraph serializer hardening) handled through load-time compat or breaking releases, not user-reported corruption. A versioned envelope with a tolerant reader is a cheap safeguard, but no upgrade-corruption bug report was found.

nodes.applicability: Current main branch of the SDK; older releases used a different, shorter sequence and the exact version where the process-group kill landed was not checked.
nodes.limitations: Source summary came through a fetch tool that paraphrased the code; quotes are from that output. Not checked against a pinned release.
nodes.text: MCP Python SDK stdio_client shutdown (_stop_server_process): close the server's stdin, wait PROCESS_TERMINATION_TIMEOUT = 2.0 s for it to exit on its own, then kill the whole process tree (SIGTERM to the process group, SIGKILL after FORCE_KILL_TIMEOUT = 2.0 s; Windows Job Object). The server is spawned in its own session/process group (POSIX) or Job Object (Windows), so descendants are killed too. A process that survives the kill is logged and abandoned, so an orphan is still possible in that last case.

nodes.applicability: MCP Python SDK stdio/HTTP clients on asyncio+anyio; reported in python-sdk, Google ADK.
nodes.limitations: No upstream python-sdk maintainer states a recommended pattern; #577 is still open with no confirmed fix; the #577 root cause is a commenter's opinion that another commenter disputed. Reports of FastMCP and langchain-mcp-adapters were not fetched.
nodes.text: The anyio cancel-scope 'different task' error arises when an async context (task group / cancel scope, e.g. inside stdio_client or an AsyncExitStack) is exited from a different asyncio task than the one that entered it, typically a cleanup task calling AsyncExitStack.aclose(); anyio's wrong-task guard raises before removing the host task from the scope. Out-of-order (non-LIFO) cleanup of several clients is a second trigger reported in #577.

nodes.limitations: Taken from one maintainer comment in an ADK issue; the python-sdk itself gives no official pattern.
nodes.text: Recommended pattern: have one dedicated long-lived owner task enter and exit the MCP client context (connect, serve requests via messages, cleanup), instead of entering in the request task and exiting elsewhere. Google ADK's maintainer called this the architectural root-cause fix (PR #4025, merged in v1.23.0, per the thread); the symptom-only fix was PR #3835.

nodes.applicability: The fetched main-branch file documents MCPToolset; MCPServerStdio was not found there, so the defaults for the older MCPServerStdio class were not confirmed from source.
nodes.limitations: Defaults are _UNSET sentinels resolved at runtime to 5 and 5*60, as reported by the fetch tool's summary rather than a verbatim line.
nodes.text: Pydantic-AI's MCP toolset (main) exposes init_timeout (initial connection plus initialize handshake; default 5 s) and read_timeout (max wait for new messages on the long-lived connection; default 5 minutes).

nodes.limitations: Only the first 100000 of 118498 chars were read.
nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK MCPServerStdio takes client_session_timeout_seconds: float | None = 5, forwarded to ClientSession as the read timeout (per-request); None and 0 disable it. In the SDK's v2 path the client runs in its own asyncio task.

nodes.applicability: Cancellation and timeout mid-run in the OpenAI SDK; Pydantic AI statement concerns its step-persistence harness, which checkpoints per step (the candidate does not).
nodes.limitations: Issue #6091 is open with no maintainer reply.
nodes.text: Per-turn session persistence leaves a window where an external effect is committed but the session has no record of it: OpenAI Agents SDK issue #6091 reproduces a cancelled run whose external ledger holds both refunds while the Session holds only the user message, so a rerun cannot see the completed effect and may repeat it. Pydantic AI's step persistence states that an in-flight step is not retried and that tools with external effects need their own idempotency or reconciliation.

nodes.limitations: Reproduced with a fake Session that stores then raises; a client-managed Session with RunState, not the built-in SQLite backend.
nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK issue #4775: if Session.add_items() commits and then raises (lost acknowledgement), a retried run appends the same logical input twice and reruns the input guardrail. A maintainer closed it as not establishing practical impact in a supported backend workflow, and said closure does not mean the code path was fixed.

nodes.applicability: Durable engines (Temporal/DBOS style) with journaled steps; not per-turn persistence.
nodes.text: Pydantic AI durable execution: a tool run with durable=False executes in workflow code and runs again on every replay, and a restarted run replays completed units from the journal and retries the one in flight. Tools kept out of the durable unit must be deterministic.

nodes.limitations: #4680 test plan uses event-gated interleavings, not a free-running repro; #4988 repro used a fake client. #4736 merge status taken from the #4680 page, not fetched. No equivalent report found for Pydantic AI or LangGraph OSS.
nodes.text: A reproducible same-session overlap bug exists in the OpenAI Agents SDK: run_compaction, triggered after every turn save, could silently delete a concurrent add_items from an overlapping Runner.run on the same session. It was fixed by maintainer PR #4736, not by #4680 itself. Concurrent pop_item calls on OpenAIConversationsSession can also return the same item (#4988; closed, maintainer asked for a real-API scenario). The sessions docs add concurrency guarantees only for the compaction wrapper, none for plain sessions.

nodes.applicability: LangSmith Agent Server; an embedded library has to implement its own policy.
nodes.text: LangGraph's four multitask strategies for two runs on one thread (reject, enqueue as default, interrupt, rollback) are documented as a LangSmith Agent Server feature, not part of the open-source framework. Interrupt can leave a started-but-unfinished tool call that the graph must clean up.

nodes.limitations: Applies to the step-persistence harness stores; the plain message_history pattern has no such guard in the pages read.
nodes.text: Pydantic AI's harness guards a conversation head against concurrent writers: a stale writer or a deleted session raises ConversationConflict; SQLite writes wait up to 30 seconds for another writer; busy detection is local, not a distributed lease, and the database must not be shared between hosts. Single process is the supported scope.

nodes.limitations: Documentation of rules, not bug reports. The OpenAI claim rests on absence from a docs page and is inference-grade.
nodes.text: Versioning of stored data differs by library. Pydantic AI step persistence: marker format is versioned, compatibility is upgrade-only, old SQLite DBs gain the new column on open. Pydantic message history is saved via ModelMessagesTypeAdapter and older histories need a load-time context flag (rebuild_unrecorded_tool_files) then a re-save. LangGraph: the latest graph applies to every thread; adding optional state fields is safe, while a type change, required field without default, or rename makes existing checkpoints fail or lose data. OpenAI Agents SDK sessions page documents no version or migration mechanism (SQLite rows are JSON; only the MongoDB backend notes legacy per-item documents remain readable).

For a single-process library saving once per completed turn, the stored-history format should carry a version marker and a tolerant reader (optional new fields, upgrade-only reads, re-save after load), as Pydantic AI does, because LangGraph documents that type changes, required fields without defaults and renames break existing checkpoints.

nodes.applicability: LiteLLM proxy/router, a vendor gateway; fallback goes to a different model group (larger window, other provider), not a retry of the same request.
nodes.limitations: Page gives no guidance on when fallback is unwise (e.g. for caller bugs); only the existence and intent of the chains.
nodes.text: LiteLLM treats context-window overflow and content-policy rejection as dedicated fallback triggers (context_window_fallbacks for ContextWindowExceededError, content_policy_fallbacks for ContentPolicyViolationError), mapped across providers; the documented use is falling back to another model or provider. This is evidence against a blanket 'never fall back on caller errors such as 400 or context length'.

nodes.limitations: Describes the default; it is configurable, so it is not a recommendation to fall back on every 4xx.
nodes.text: Pydantic AI FallbackModel's default trigger is ModelAPIError (4xx/5xx and pre-response connection failures/timeouts), explicitly including rejected requests such as bad credentials, rejected model name and context-window overflow, on the reasoning that another model may accept what the first rejected.

Refinement of the fallback policy: context-length (and content-policy) errors are fallback-worthy only when the fallback target differs in a way that can fix them (larger window, other provider policy); generic 4xx caller errors (malformed request, auth on the same credential) are not fixed by another model. Both LiteLLM and Pydantic AI treat context overflow as a fallback case, so @C45 should be narrowed to 'not on caller bugs', not 'not on context length'.

nodes.limitations: Single user issue report (reproduction by the author), not a maintainer-confirmed analysis on the page fetched. Scenario is two servers resuming one session; a single-process host serialising turns per session avoids it.
nodes.text: Google ADK 1.24.0 changed DatabaseSessionService.append_event() from raising ValueError on a stale session to reloading the session and appending anyway; with two concurrent run_async calls on one session this interleaves events, the LLM sees duplicate/contradictory tool calls and responses, and history is corrupted. Reported affected versions >=1.24.0 (1.24.0, 1.25.0, 1.26.0); last working 1.23.0.

nodes.applicability: Spanner dialect of DatabaseSessionService.
nodes.limitations: Dialect-specific; second independent report of concurrent-turn problems in ADK.
nodes.text: ADK issue #4771 reports that overlapping requests on one session (a new turn arriving while the previous turn still writes events) make the new turn start with missing session state; a maintainer notes concurrent append_event() writes can trigger OCC aborts even on pure reads (Spanner dialect). Page does not mention duplicate tool calls; those are in #4751.

nodes.limitations: Fix commit not read; whether main restored the ValueError on stale sessions is unverified.
nodes.text: ADK PR #4752 (optimistic concurrency via an event sequence number, rejecting stale updates with 'The session has been modified in storage. Please reload the session before appending events.') was closed unmerged on 2026-07-06; the maintainer closed it saying #4751 was already fixed in main by commit b8e7647. The content of that fix was not verified (commit page returned HTTP 503).

Concurrent turns on one persisted session are a recurring failure source across frameworks (ADK stale-session reload-and-continue; OpenAI SDK concurrent add_items deletion), so a single-process library should serialise turns per session (or use a version check on save) rather than rely on the storage layer.

nodes.limitations: Reference page for the version current on 2026-11-20.
nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK MCPServerManager defaults connect_timeout_seconds=10.0 and cleanup_timeout_seconds=10.0 (None disables, zero rejected), with strict=False, drop_failed_servers=True and connect_in_parallel=False. This is a manager-level connect timeout, distinct from the 5 s client_session_timeout_seconds per-request timeout in @C42.

nodes.limitations: The last sentence (non-UTF-8 bytes) is our inference from the utf8 description, not a quoted statement.
nodes.text: Pydantic v2 ser_json_bytes and val_json_bytes both default to 'utf8' (options utf8, base64, hex); to get an equal value after a serialise/validate round trip they must be set equal. val_json_bytes was added in v2.9. With the utf8 default, arbitrary (non-UTF-8) bytes do not round-trip safely, so persisted conversation JSON containing bytes should use base64 on both sides.

alternatives: Item-level append protocol (OpenAI Session get_items/add_items/pop_item/clear): trimming and summarizing rewrite history, so append-only items fit badly, and its pop/compaction paths had race bugs
Revisioned record plus entries log with optimistic concurrency (Pydantic AI ConversationStore): built for concurrent writers and forks, which a single-instance host does not need yet
nodes.chosen: Keep a whole-record save/load protocol per conversation id (the existing Checkpointer shape), storing a ConversationRecord with format_version, messages and cumulative usage; serialize with a pydantic TypeAdapter configured with base64 bytes and a tolerant reader that accepts older versions and raises a typed error on an unknown newer one. ConversationAgent holds a per-conversation asyncio.Lock from load to save across the whole turn; a second turn on the same conversation waits for the first.
nodes.decision_rule: If the host runs several replicas or concurrent writers per conversation, add an expected_revision argument to save and raise a typed conflict error, as Pydantic AI does.
nodes.rationale: ConversationAgent already saves the whole history after each completed turn, and its context strategies trim or summarize history, which rewrites it; a record-level save matches that. Pydantic AI stores a conversation record with usage beside messages; versioned formats with upgrade-only readers are the documented practice; OpenAI's item-level append store has had concurrency bugs around pop and compaction.
nodes.title: Conversation store: protocol shape and stored format
nodes.tradeoffs: Simple to implement for a host (two methods); rewrites the whole history per turn; turns on one conversation are serialized in process, with no conflict detection across processes.
nodes.uncertainty: Medium: rests on single-process and bounded-history assumptions.

alternatives: LangGraph-style saver (put, put_writes, get_tuple, list, durability modes): needed only for parallel branches and checkpoint history
Drop workflow persistence as Pydantic AI did: the feature exists with tests and works for sequential graphs
nodes.chosen: Reuse the same save/load protocol and JSON codec for WorkflowCheckpoint, keyed by run id, keeping only the latest checkpoint after each completed node; no pending-writes, history listing or durability modes.
nodes.decision_rule: If parallel nodes or checkpoint history are added, move to a put/put_writes/list protocol.
nodes.rationale: Resume after a completed step is the requirement; LangGraph's put_writes and list exist for parallel super-steps and time travel, which the platform's sequential graph does not have; Pydantic AI dropped arbitrary graph-state snapshotting because of parallel execution.
nodes.title: Workflow checkpoint store
nodes.tradeoffs: Minimal surface; no time travel or checkpoint history. The workflow state type must be pydantic-serializable, and custom objects in state are a compatibility risk across upgrades; an agent node that crashes mid-node is replayed from the last completed node, with the replay semantics of D7.

alternatives: aiosqlite: native async but a new dependency for a small gain
Postgres: needs a server and is the multi-replica option, out of scope
JSON files per key: no atomic multi-record writes and poor listing
nodes.chosen: One SQLite backend on the standard-library sqlite3 module, under integrations/, with one key-value table (namespace, key, format_version, JSON payload, updated_at); each call opens its own connection inside asyncio.to_thread (no shared connection, so no check_same_thread issue), with WAL mode; the in-memory store stays for tests.
nodes.decision_rule: If the host runs several replicas, add a Postgres backend behind the same protocol.
nodes.rationale: OpenAI Agents SDK ships SQLite as its default local session store and LangGraph ships SQLite savers for local workflows; Pydantic AI documents that its SQLite stores must not be shared between hosts, which matches the single-instance constraint; the standard library avoids a new dependency.
nodes.title: Reference backend
nodes.tradeoffs: Single-host only; thread offloading adds small latency.

alternatives: Pre-request token counting (Pydantic AI count_tokens_before_request): an extra provider call, supported by only some providers
Turn or step caps only (OpenAI max_turns, LangGraph recursion_limit): the platform already has max_iterations and it does not bound tokens
Spend limit in currency: not requested; needs a price table per model
nodes.chosen: An opt-in UsageLimits value (input, output and total tokens, and request count) with a run scope and a conversation scope, off by default; checked before each LLM call against accumulated usage and after each response; raises a typed UsageLimitExceeded carrying the scope, the limit and the usage. Conversation usage is stored in the conversation record and is updated even when a turn fails: a failed turn saves a usage-only update (messages unchanged) before the error propagates. Documented as a soft cap.
nodes.rationale: Pydantic AI is the only library of the three with token limits, checks them before requests and after responses, and raises a typed error; it documents that the crossing request completes, so the cap is soft; OpenAI and LangGraph cap only turns or steps, and a call-count cap is not a spend cap. Conversation scope needs usage carried across runs.
nodes.title: Opt-in usage limits
nodes.tradeoffs: Soft cap: one call can overshoot unless the host also sets a per-request max_tokens, the cheap hard bound on output. Fallback attempts add tokens inside the cap, and a failed attempt that reports no usage is not counted.
nodes.uncertainty: Medium: accuracy depends on provider-reported usage.

alternatives: Fall back on every API error (Pydantic AI default): a malformed request fails on each model in turn and multiplies cost
Re-raise every permanent error (audit F6 fix text): a bad key on the primary, or a prompt too long for it, blocks a fallback that would work
Never fall back on context length (first draft of this decision): contradicted by LiteLLM and Pydantic AI practice
nodes.chosen: One classifier in core sorts errors into transient (timeout, connection, 429, 5xx), caller errors (malformed request, schema or argument error), context-length, content-policy and provider-scoped permanent (auth, permission, model not found). Only transient errors are retried, in one layer, including the batch methods. The fallback chain moves on for transient, provider-scoped and content-policy errors; on a context-length error it moves on only to a provider whose model has a larger context window, else re-raises; it re-raises caller errors at once.
nodes.rationale: Retry layers multiply, and SDK retries skip 401 and 404. Falling back on every error (Pydantic AI and LangChain defaults) makes a malformed request fail on each model and multiplies spend. But another model can fix some rejections: Pydantic AI falls back on rejected credentials, model names and context overflow, and LiteLLM has dedicated context-window and content-policy fallbacks.
nodes.title: LLM error policy: retry and fallback
nodes.tradeoffs: Each adapter maps vendor errors into five classes; the chain needs each model context window to apply the context-length rule.
nodes.uncertainty: Medium: depends on vendor error codes being distinguishable; content-policy mapping varies by vendor.

alternatives: A dedicated owner task per server (Google ADK fix, Agents SDK parallel connect): needed only when clients open and close in different tasks, which the lifespan does not do
nodes.chosen: Bound connect plus initialize with a configurable startup timeout, default 10 s (the OpenAI Agents SDK manager default; Pydantic AI uses 5 s, tight for servers started through npx or uvx); keep the existing per-call tool timeout (mcp_tool_timeout, 60 s); at shutdown close every client in reverse order, each close guarded so one failure does not skip the rest, in the same task that opened them (the app lifespan).
nodes.decision_rule: If clients are opened lazily per request or closed from another task, move each client into an owner task.
nodes.rationale: Both libraries bound the startup handshake (Pydantic AI init_timeout 5 s; OpenAI MCPServerManager connect_timeout_seconds 10 s), separate from the per-request read timeout. The MCP SDK already kills the server process tree on close; the anyio cancel-scope error appears when a client is closed from another task or out of order; the Agents SDK manager cleans up in reverse order on the same task.
nodes.title: MCP client lifecycle
nodes.tradeoffs: A slow-starting server fails startup unless the timeout is raised.

alternatives: Per-step checkpoints inside the agent loop: excluded by scope, left to the capabilities brainstorm
An effect ledger with idempotency keys (Pydantic AI harness annotate_tool_effect), as the disconfirming review recommended for effectful tools: more machinery than a single-instance host needs now
A stable turn id saved before the turn starts, passed to tools: cheap, but adds a write per turn and a tool-context contract; revisit with the capabilities brainstorm
nodes.chosen: A failed or cancelled turn saves no messages (only its usage, per D4); the host retries from the last saved turn. Tool calls and results are saved with the completed turn. The library offers no deduplication handle: a replayed turn gets new model-generated tool-call ids, so tools with external effects must derive their own idempotency key from host state. Documented as the top risk.
nodes.rationale: Per-turn persistence leaves a window where an external effect is committed but unrecorded, reproduced in OpenAI Agents SDK issues; Pydantic AI's step persistence also leaves in-flight effects to the tool's own idempotency. Per-step checkpoints are out of scope by the human's decision.
nodes.title: Replay semantics of a failed turn
nodes.tradeoffs: An effectful tool can run twice after a crash mid-turn.
nodes.uncertainty: Medium: depends on what tools hosts register.

nodes.text: What is the exact v1 pydantic_graph BaseStatePersistence/NodeSnapshot/EndSnapshot API and semantics (superseded by removal in V2)? Does PostgresSaver commit writes and checkpoints atomically?

Fetch the primary GitHub issues for the anyio cancel-scope bug (langchain-mcp-adapters #99, fastmcp #348, python-sdk) and the MCP Python SDK stdio_client shutdown sequence (stdin close, terminate, kill timeouts); verify orphan-subprocess behavior.

Is there a reproducible report of two concurrent turns on one session_id corrupting or losing history in Pydantic AI, OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph? Searches found only thread-safety and partial-failure bugs.

Is there a concrete bug report that a token limit is bypassed by streaming, or not covered by handoffs or sub-agents in OpenAI Agents SDK? Not found; only Pydantic AI docs on post-response checks and shared usage.
Does a fallback chain mask real bugs or cause cost spikes in practice? Only the docs-level cost accounting (c6) was found, no post-mortem.

What does the official LangGraph durable-execution page (docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/durable-execution) say verbatim about wrapping side effects in tasks and idempotency? The fetch returned other pages in this run, so only secondary summaries were seen.

topic: Runtime state and cost limits in embeddable Python agent libraries
